utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] In this final section where I intend to highlight the materials that relate to the third item that I indicated yesterday of importance, namely the personality and character of Fatmir Limaj. This section has of course a double relevance. And in a sense what I would like to do is to run the materials in tandem in relation to two areas, the first being the one I began with yesterday, namely its relevance to the substantive liability within the indictment in the way that I describe, namely it involves anticipating here that there has been this metamorphosis of a man from responsibility to thorough irresponsibility. The second point that he would be risking the vision that he had for Kosovo by these actions and his own credibility. That's on the one side, substantive liability. On the other side of course all these materials have a considerable bearing on the final matter the Prosecution addressed to you yesterday, namely sentencing. And what we've done in order to again hopefully assist and reduce the amount of time that is taken up orally with you is to produce overnight a skeleton of this part, which I believe you now have and the Prosecution have. I again -- as with other skeletons, I don't intend to read them out but to concentrate on one or two matters within it. May I ask you in that context if you be kind enough to turn to page 5 because we say one of the crucial factors that you would want to have in mind, if there is -- and I make it clear publicly we're putting this on the basis that this is contingent, plainly, upon a finding of guilt and that is the only reason we are dealing with it now. It may be not easy to understand why the Defence would be addressing sentencing publicly when, in fact, of course our primary submissions have been that of course Mr. Limaj is not guilty. But we appreciate that you do on occasion require observations about the possibility of sentence. So in deference to that, we are in fact putting forward some, we hope, constructive factors. The one I light upon is the one we've headed reconciliation. I light upon that because it links entirely with the fourth objective which I began with yesterday, the objective of reconciliation as far as this Tribunal is concerned. And we say that that is of particular significance in this case because, firstly, we say there is indisputable evidence that this attempt at reconciliation by Fatmir Limaj was in the face of - and of course his return from Switzerland - was in the face of a decade of unimaginable oppression and desecration which I described in detail yesterday, perpetrated by the Serb regime. And that what he did when he came back was effectively an active last resort to protect civilians. And it is through the protection of civilians that again is indisputable what he did in the mountain areas. Again, I touched on it yesterday. And also finally, of course, his attempts -- and I'll highlight some of those, at a political reconciliation once the war was over, again is indisputable. So those three matters in the context of reconciliation. A defence and protection force serving civilians thousands holed up in the valleys to avoid, themselves, being destroyed by the Serb onslaught in 1998 and his political initiatives after the war, again we say unchallenged during the trial and indisputable place him in a very unique situation. Now, what are the materials, therefore, that underlie these two aspects? One related to liability, one related to any sentencing that may arise later and if it does. The first material, if I may put it that way, is the witness Fadil Bajraktari. He was the mountain teacher and he was the one who described -- he was amongst a number who you may recall have taken the trouble to come here. It's often very easy to put something on paper and then for it to be relied upon in that sense, but he took the trouble to come and he sat before you. You may remember an emotionally charged day in which he recalled what had happened in that autumn period to the children, particularly the children, and the way in which shelter was provided and assisted by Fatmir Limaj, food was provided, again assisted by Fatmir Limaj; schooling was provided. You saw the photographs of the makeshift tents and the conditions under which this was done. Medical supplies were provided, assisted by Fatmir Limaj. And most of all, perhaps, and something which he has contrived to do throughout and again it has a stark contrast to the allegations in the indictment, is to provide hope and provide inspiration. And he did it in a particular way for this individual and I merely quote one passage from the transcript of his evidence. It comes, if you need the reference to see any more of what he said but you may remember it, it's transcript 6886 to 6887. One of the final questions I asked him was in fact what difference this has all made to his life, never mind the children's. And he said: "He," that meaning Fatmir, "has influenced my life a lot. I want to go to an earlier period. In March of 1998, I was very sick. I had a kidney problem. I was in Pristina, and I went back to my village. The doctor I saw for my problem," and he names the doctor, Dervishi, "and he proposed me to have an operation in order to become well again. The situation in that hospital were not good. The conditions were almost horrible, so this operation remained an idea. So in these very difficult moments, I decided to go to my village. I wanted to be close to my family, where I belonged. "So also when we went to the mountains, I was feeling worse and worse. A medical team came from the Red Cross, from Geneva, and they took me -- they wanted to take me abroad to be cured, but Fatmir's idea to have a school to teach the children made me refuse that idea. I told those doctors that I won't come. I decided to stay with the children. I proposed them to take two young mothers who were about to give birth. "I couldn't leave those children there even if I would feel well again and my kidneys would become better. I did not want that life. I wanted to be close to the children because my life was with them. "Believe me, the miracle happened. I did not go to the doctor again. I did not need that surgery any more. The kidney stones that I had, I passed them out myself until February 1999. So I did not need the surgery any more. "That's what happened to me. And today I'm as fit as a fiddle. I don't suffer any more. But it was Fatmir who taught me how to become a teacher, to become a teacher of those children, 'The teacher of the mountain' as they called me." A haunting testimony of one individual, but of course hope and inspiration often springs not only eternal but from the individual that is affected in this way. This was a man, Fatmir Limaj, who had his hands very much on his heart and on the people he wanted to help. After this, and I don't go through the detail because you have it already, that is post-Rambouillet and the conference in Paris in 1999, I just want to highlight some of the other things he did, that is Fatmir Limaj, and we do it with considerable emphasis because of the way the Prosecution suggest in some manner that this -- this individual, Fatmir Limaj, is an opportunist who happens to be forced to do these things; we say not. He became deputy minister of defence of the provisional department after the departure of the Serb forces and the arrival of NATO forces and you may recall that he participated in talks concerning demilitarisation. Really, this is extremely important for all the reasons I explained this afternoon. Demilitarisation of an area which had seen a lot of conflict of one kind or another. And within one week, within one week, agreement had been reached for a process of normalisation. Between June and September, three months, he helped to disarm the very people who you might imagine would be reluctant to be disarmed, given what they had faced and given the possibilities in all these situations that they're frightened will be resumed in the future. But -- he wasn't alone, but he was part of a team of people who helped a smooth transition, and we say that is very relevant to both of these tandem headings I've indicated, liability and the future should there happen to be sentencing. But he didn't stop at that. The talks continued. They were in London, Brussels, Rome, and Washington, because the ultimate objective wasn't just demilitarisation, it was the creation of a new force, of course very much in a sense exactly the reason he'd returned to Kosovo: a protection force for Kosovo which still exists. But to provide that, to create it, there had to be a clear mandate and a clear set of parameters as to how that would operate. And a final agreement was signed with Generals Clark and Jackson, names known obviously to Your Honours. This was a process he described to you, he participated in and helped to achieve. And he said this, transcript T6057, Fatmir himself, and in a sense it is a remarkable transition. He said: "You can imagine, Your Honours," effectively, that to go from an army that had been fighting certainly in 1999 a hugely superior force, to go from that to disbanding that army and creating, he didn't use these words a peace corps, because that's what it is, but the words he said, perhaps an exaggeration, had "never occurred in the history of mankind." Well, that may not be entirely right, but it is a remarkable achievement and therefore something we would ask you to bear in mind on the two fronts I've suggested. But that again didn't end his path, didn't end what he was trying to do. Because if in fact he wanted to curry favour, if in fact he was merely an opportunist, the one thing he wouldn't do is what he then did do, because having undoubtedly fought the Serbs as part of the exercise of the return from Switzerland, he then entered with equal vigour the democratic process which was in its infancy at that point, the formation of political parties and elections. He became secretary for public relations for the PDK. The Kosovo Assembly was being converted effectively into a parliament or the kind of institution that is known in many other western democracies. And his commitment to that has been recognised by a large number of people, recognised clearly by the prime minister of the time who also took the trouble to come here and indicated that he'd played - that is Fatmir - the most crucial role after the war and the most constructive person. And it's -- really does behoove you to recall these words when considering the two fronts I've indicated because it's very easy in these circumstances merely, as it were, to disappear into the background, take a back seat. But he didn't do that. And no doubt there are people in Kosovo, some, who weren't so happy that he took this courageous stand. And what the prime minister in fact told you, this is at transcript 6778: "I'd like to say," that's to you, "that this man had the courage and the bravery since the very first days after the war to extend his hand to the representatives of the Serb community." Imagine, the enemy; imagine the end of the Second World War and extending the hand of friendship to the German oppressor. That's essentially what he was doing, unlike some other politicians who were rather hesitant at that time to do the same. So I have always admired him for his courage and his readiness to do that after all what happened in Kosovo, to find the strength and work towards reconciliation. "Mr. Limaj is missing" from "the political life in Kosova and to parliament. The minority communities have lost a powerful supporter in their fight for their rights in Kosova in general, and in parliament in particular." And it therefore comes as no surprise, and he mentioned it, that there was in an earlier stage in the proceedings before the Tribunal a minority statement from those ethnic minorities in support of Fatmir Limaj. But more importantly, even, that that, in other words even if you may inwardly feel, well, those are his supporters, they are not all his supporters but they support his vision of a multi-racial,multicultural and inclusive and pluralist society. It is in fact the internationalists, if I may call them that, who provide the largest commendation. And perhaps if you need a reliable basis, unlike, as we say, the unreliability of much of the Prosecution case, a reliable basis for assessing this man, it comes from those people. Since a number of them are in the final brief, I don't recite them all only by name so that it can be clear who we are dealing with here. One of the witnesses in these proceedings was a man called Jan Kickert, an Austrian diplomat who was the acting personal representative in Pristina to the European Union High Representative For Common and Security Policy, Foreign policy and also the Security General of the Council of Europe. He had a very high regard for Fatmir Limaj, for his openness, for his attempts at reconciliation and for his attempts at inclusivity, all terms that everyone uses. This is not somebody who's pretending because these are individuals who cannot be taken in easily and who make assessments regularly. And we say they are genuine assessments. Peter Bouckaert of the Human Rights Watch, similarly. Dan Everts who was three years at the head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, OSCE. Also it was clear from the evidence of a witness who came slightly later has provided you, and if you need the reference it's DL14, with a letter which was written in April 2003. And may I just read a paragraph from that letter because again it is compelling material. And he's describing Fatmir Limaj and how he knew him during those three years and the reconstruction of the region in which of course that organisation, concerned with democracy and institutions of democracy, was concerned. He said this: "As an active member of the Kosovo Assembly, subsequently transformed into the democratically elected parliament, Mr. Limaj has always advocated inclusive,conciliatory governance stressing the importance of compromise and accommodation. He forcefully argued in favour of his party," the PDK, "joining the joint interim administrative structure, including Serb participation, which was crucial at the time for achieving broad-based agreement on executive rule by UN administration. "He has also taken a firm stand against ethnic violence and nationalist extremism inside Kosovo as well as with regard to the near civil war in the neighbouring former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and southern Serbia." The letter goes on, but you may regard that as an impressive testimonial. And I turn to Carolyn McCool who had once again taken the trouble to come here from Canada and did not rely purely on what she had already put in her report. And again what she had to say, given her position within the same organisation for security and cooperation and that she'd been stationed in Kosovo from August 1999 through to September 2002. She was particularly familiar, you may feel, with Kosovo and the difficulties of a post-war reconciliation and reconstruction. She was in Pristina between the beginning of 2001 and the end of her final period in 2002. And it was in that period that she came to know Fatmir Limaj and his support for the institutes of -- institutions of government and civil society, and in particular his support for the rule of law. And this is what she said, and there are a number of citations, but it's -- the transcript begins at 6706. And I just cull some of them because again we say they are compelling and impressive: "Mr. Limaj became one of those leaders in Kosovo who I trusted implicitly." How many people could that be said of who stand before you or sit before you in these Tribunals? "We would talk about politics in which I found it very difficult to talk to a lot of people, in a way that was open and candid and in which he would disclose the difficulties that he had as a leader." And then she goes on to tabulate the difficulties she had as a foreigner. And then on the next page 6707, having described the enormity of the problems: "Mr. Limaj approached these problems which were enormous and remained enormous. The whole question of the development of a multi-ethnic society in Kosovo is one which is moving very slowly, very slowly, in its resolution. Mr. Limaj's approach, more and more, as I knew him was to try and resolve that -- those problems, that host of problems, by talking to people. And by that, I don't simply mean foreigners like me. I mean by talking with other representatives of other ethnic communities, most notably the Kosovo-Serbian community. And of course it's the relationship between the Albanian and the Serbian people which is at the heart of the history of Kosovo since at least the 1980s," and which as I highlighted yesterday remains at the root in the difficulties in the recent publicity of the final status talks. "Mr. Limaj, in my view, and in the period I knew him developed qualities of leadership, which included a vision of a multi-ethnic Kosovo. And he" didn't do this by [sic] "simply sitting in his office and by talking to his PDK colleagues, but by leaving his offices and talking with Serbs as well as with representatives of other ethnic communities, as well as foreigners such as myself. "So he was one of those people that Serbian leaders were prepared to talk to and he was prepared to talk to them." She then gave examples. And then she gave this passage, again very telling in the context of this case: "He grew in stature as a leader, was balanced in his division of a developing multi-ethnic society against some of the views of some of his constituents, which was still locked in the sort of historical embrace of antipathy, indeed hatred, at some levels. And he was indeed moving beyond that and prepared to talk to people about how they were going to make this thing work in the end. And this was, in my view, one of the things that was most interesting about Mr. Limaj, is that this was not done simply for the benefit of the donor community;" we say in contrast to the arguments of the Prosecution yesterday, was not done to get the benefits of "pleasing the donors in a post-conflict situation. One of the reasons that I felt continually interested in talking with him was because it was clear that he was doing this because he was developing a vision of Kosovo for the future which would serve all of the people of that land." And then finally she said: "I remember one meeting at which Mr. Limaj in fact proposed a whole plan of action whereby the Assembly of Kosovo could engage in a dialogue with similar bodies in surrounding countries and jurisdictions - with other parliamentarians, basically - to work on -- he mentioned economic development as being the greatest priority on a regional basis as well as other issues of mutual concern. And he and these Serbian leaders were in fact in agreement on this kind of plan of action. This was -- this was in the -- this was just before I left Kosovo in September 2002. And indeed, had Mr. Limaj come -- not come to be here," meaning before you, "I believe that he probably would have pursued those plans. And it may be that in the end something comes of that; we shall see." And of course the hopes of the community he served plainly do hang upon plans and visions of that kind. And it's a vision which of course some in politics and Martin Luther King would call a dream. Interestingly, in a book published by now an international -- the first international Booker prize winner this year, Ismail Kadare, an Albanian writer. He wrote a book entitled The Palace of Dreams. And in fact it was the description, no doubt, of a regime against which he'd set his own face and no doubt Fatmir Limaj would have set his face against a totalitarian regime rather than a democratic one. But in the book he describes the need for master dreams [sic], in other words: "Those who do have have a facility to have visions that will govern the destiny of states." If I may end what I have to say to you with in fact the final observations of Fatmir Limaj himself about this vision. It's quite short. It's T6064. He said this to you: "I very much believe that if we don't take the initiative of creating, building trust amongst us, nothing will succeed no matter what UNMIK does. I regret to say it, but in this case in Kosovo we should have brave people, people who are willing to assume responsibilities upon their own shoulders, and not to do things only for the sake of the international community, as the case is today in Kosovo. We should do things because this is in the interest and for the benefit of the people, not because of the international community wanting us to do that. Standards are for the people, for the sides. They are for the ones who build life. In a word, they was some of the objectives of my orientation. I think brave politicians are still missing in Kosovo, politicians who should assume responsibility for the good of the people. But unfortunately, the ones we have think only of their own interests and this has created tension in my country. This is my personal view." So may I say in summary, therefore, this is a remarkable man who sits here today, a remarkable man who we say was not capable and did not commit the crimes as alleged by the Prosecution. But bearing in mind, of course, that the final judgement lies with you, if in fact, contrary to our submissions, you feel he has played a part in the allegations made against him, then we say in the light of all this material, in the light of the oppression and the desecration that he faced and his community faced, and in the light of the undoubted help that he has provided to thousands of civilians during the war, any sentence in the bracket that was mentioned yesterday should be, we submit, at the very lowest level of that bracket in order to mark both reconciliation and his role in it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Mr. Bala, members of the Prosecution, and my colleagues. About a year ago I was on a plane travelling from Vienna to Pristina, a place that I'd never been before. And as sometimes I do on a plane, I decided to speak to the person next to me. We engaged in conversation. He turned out to be somebody who lived in the United States who was a soccer coach, something that some of you would call football, others would call soccer. And something that I was rather interested in because my son had played soccer from a very, very early age and this gentleman was someone who was training young men and women across the country. He also was from Kosovo and had had the privilege years before of playing on one of the few teams that was able to succeed internationally. And he was somewhat proud of that, as well he should be. We had coffee with each on the plane. He showed me photographs of his family. He showed me photographs of himself with other people. We were in extremely close proximity to each other. When the plane landed we promised that we would meet with each other, perhaps have a cup of coffee with each other in Pristina, both staying at the Grand Hotel. I missed him a couple of days, he missed me a couple of days, notes were exchanged at the lobby. Then finally we were able to meet and I spent about a half an hour, perhaps more, with not only him but with his family and some of his friends where we exchanged the kind of pleasantries that are exchanged between human beings. It was a very, very pleasurable experience, calm, and one that I commented on when I left Pristina. Nine months later I was once again in Pristina. I was walking down the street and somebody called my name, Gregor, and I looked and there he was. And I was -- I was so, so pleased to see him. At the time I was walking down the street close to the Grand Hotel with my co-counsel. I said, Come on, Richard, come meet this man. He's a great guy, Ed. He's a wonderful human being. You should really know him. He's a great soccer player, he's done much for young people around the world and I think you would enjoy him. We went and we spoke to each other for a few minutes and then went our separate ways, understanding that we would meet at the airport because he was leaving that day, as was I. I spoke a little bit to Richard about this man, not much. We went about our day and then when we got to the airport I saw him again and I went up to him and I said, Hi, Ed, how are you? And he said, Mr. Guy-Smith, do you know who I am? And I went, Yes, you are -- then I went Oh my God, oh my goodness. He said, I didn't mean to embarrass you, but you know who I am. I said, Yes, of course. You are the gentleman who I have been to the Detention Unit more than once, more than twice, more than three times. You are the gentleman who was my translator to talk to Mr. Bala. Now, if I was called to testify and if there was any question at all up to the moment that I was standing at the airport and this man said to me, do you know what I am? My answer would have been of course I know who he is. This is Ed, the man who plays soccer. And if somebody had asked me the question, well how sure are you? My response would have been simple, 100 per cent. You don't even have to think about the words would have been; you can tell by my actions themselves that my response would have been. 100 per cent. 100 per cent accurate, I would have thought; 100 per cent wrong. It has been said with regard to the issue of eyewitness testimony that "implicit in the acceptance of this testimony is solid evidence is the assumption that the human mind is a precise recorder and storer of events." Unfortunately it's not. "To be mistaken about details is not the result of a bad memory, but of the normal functioning of human memory." As we have seen, "human remembering does not work like a video recorder or a movie camera. New information, oftentimes misleading information, is not only added to memory, it actually alters the conduct -- content of what the subject is able to remember." The upshot is that even honest eyewitnesses who try to be objective, who believe what they are relating, may in fact remember incorrectly and produce misinformation. Courts have recognised this. Courts have recognised the frailty of eyewitness identification, and this Chamber itself has commented on how an analysis of identification is something that will require serious scrutiny and great, great care. Most of the people who have testified here with regard to the identity of Shala have recounted a tall man, a dark man, a man with bad teeth. Few have remembered the colour of his eyes. As a matter of fact, I believe that only one mentioned that his eyes were blue/green, somewhat of an unusual colour. Most of the individuals who claim that the man who they had unfortunate, indeed unfortunate, experiences with, who they knew as Shala, who they transferred to the name of Bala, admitted in one fashion or another that information came to them which clearly, if we are to analyse the issue of their identification, was either influenced, unreliable, or highly suggestive. Some claim to see him on television. Some claim that they were told that Shala, through rumour, was Bala. And the reason they knew that was because his father, a well-known singer in the region, was somebody that they were all familiar with. Now, in the context of what has occurred during these proceedings, one of the things that is terribly clear is that there is more than one Shala on the ground and in the field at Lapusnik, and that's those with the pseudonym Shala. At Lapusnik we have heard of two. One of them came to testify; he was a tall man. He had no moustache. He worked at the compound where the Prosecution has put this prison camp. And he was identified by, among others, as being a guard, at least initially, L-64. For a moment I wish to give you an image because thus far in the discussions that have been had, everybody has suggested that we know what reasonable doubt is, that we all are familiar with the concept and the standards that are to be applied. And of course you being judges, versed in the law, left with the duty of not only here finding law but also facts, I for a moment will ask you as a jury to consider this, because for the moment that's what you are: You are a jury, a fact-finding jury. And what I would suggest to you with regard to the issue of reasonable doubt and how to define reasonable doubt is that reasonable doubt, to have something proved to you beyond a reasonable doubt requires the kind of certainty and confidence that you would have in conducting the most Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. important of your own affairs. That your reliance on the representation made, that your reliance on the evidence given, that your reliance on the word spoken is such that you would be confident to place your safety, your life, your welfare or of those who are close to you in the hands of that information. Because you well know that at times I'm going to be talking about the medical aspects of my client's situation, may I suggest to you that when viewing the notion of reasonable doubt you consider that you are walking into a surgery. The surgeons are the witnesses who have testified. The lead surgeon for the Prosecution, for the moment, is L-64. L-64 will take the appropriate tool, and in so doing he will begin surgery on you. Are you confident? Are you comfortable? Would you rely on that man operating on you? I think not. I think not. Before you go under, you have a discussion with him. You say, Tell me a bit about yourself. He explains to you who he is. Well, at the moment I'm a recovered heroin addict, but I have that under control. As a matter of fact, it really never was a problem. I've engaged in a series of criminal behaviours, but they don't really affect what's about to happen to you. And when it comes to issues that are important, when it comes to matters that are critical for your consideration, I lie or deviate from the truth or hide the truth or place others in harm's way for reasons that I am not able to articulate. You speak with him a bit more. You say, Are you sure you're up to this job? Because that's what the Prosecution is asking, I think. You will recall in their words he is the only member of the KLA who was willing, and apparently that willingness has no conditions attached to it, to come and tell you about the truth. That's what they're saying to you. What truth? Well, the truth that they believe - and by "they" I mean the Prosecution believes - is necessary for their theory. And I digress for a very, very brief moment. There's a notion and it's one that I know you're all familiar with. It's the one that's in the Statute and the one that's in all jurisdictions, domestic and international, and that's the presumption of innocence. And in those jurisdictions where there are juries and there is a discussion with the jury beforehand to determine whether they're qualified, one of the questions that's asked is: As you -- at the beginning -- As you sit here right now, prospective a near [phoen] person, what do you think? Is the accused guilty or innocent? And oftentimes the answer that is heard which they believe is the correct answer is: They're innocent until proven guilty, which makes sense. But when there's an inquiry about what that means, innocent until proven guilty, and there's an opportunity to discuss with people, what does that mean to you? How do you feel about that? What do you think about that? The answer is always inevitably the same: they're innocent right now and when the Prosecution puts on evidence, then they're guilty. Now. Not right now this very minute, but now. After these submissions are over is when the wall -- and by that I mean the wall that is required for the presumption of innocence has to be constructed. That's when the attitude that you - because I'm talking to you for the moment as a jury - this is the time when you construct that presumption of innocence. This is the time when you say, have they proven to my satisfaction this case? Can I rely in those matters that are of the most important to me? Because in fact, the decisions you make are the most important to these men, and certainly to Mr. Bala. Now, I'm not asking for that analysis to have any emotion, none. I'm asking for that analysis to be, in fact, objective. During the cross-examination -- well, actually during the examination of L-64 and the cross-examination of L-64, he revealed that he had an off-the-record discussion with Mr. Lehtinen concerning his statement to him. Now, the reason that he had this off-the-record discussion was, as he put it, his security concerns. And Mr. Lehtinen assured him that he had nothing to worry about in that regard and that he could be confident that if he wanted to change any of his answers, that the following would be considered. And this is at page 4783: "I hope that we can continue and I hope there's something earlier -- earlier in the interview that," and I use L-64 as opposed to a specific name, "has answered in a different way because of this concern that he had that this can now be corrected and will not be considered as him changing his statement." Because of his security concerns, he can say something different and we, the Prosecution, will not consider this to be a change of his statement. Well and good. So be it. I don't believe, quite frankly, in the search for the truth. I don't believe that if what we are engaged in here is an equal and, shall we say, dispassionate investigation that such a position is particularly advisable, however. One would think that he had said something in his statement previously that directly related to, perhaps, where he lived, who he was associated with, who he had dealt with, something along those lines. Did not. The only thing that changed in the statement that this man made in his interviews in May when Shala was a tall guard with a limp was the identity of the guard. Nothing else changed. "Q. So with regard to your ability to change your statement to either include or -- information or exclude information that you previously had dealt with in your interviews in May and the earlier part of your interview in June, certainly by this time the conversation came about there was nothing further that you were going to change, was there? "A. There was nothing to change either in May or in June. The fact -- the only difference is in May I didn't want to talk about Shala." Well, what does that have to do with security? What happened in that off-the-record discussion? What did L-64 learn or surmise then that he decided to point the finger from where it had been for some period of time to Haradin Bala? By that time it was clear that the investigation was focussed on Haradin Bala. If there was any question about whether or not there was a focus an Haradin Bala, all you have to do is remember the words of Mr. Kereakes. Mr. Kereakes, who was the first individual to engage in the investigation, an investigation inherited by Mr. Lehtinen, who in his statement indicated that he had shown a photograph to L-96 -- not L-64, L-96. He had shown a photograph to L-96 -- I should say photo spread, and that he had picked out Haradin Bala as Shala. But that never happened. And Mr. Kereakes admitted that never happened. He never showed any picture, any photo spread. But the initial architect of the investigation was willing to state without any compunction whatsoever that he didn't engage in activity. That he never engaged in. That he had achieved a result that was never achieved. Perhaps Mr. Kereakes should be the anaesthesiologist. In the context of identification, it has been suggested to you that one should look at independent corroborative facts as a basis for assistance. Shall we contrast the testimony then of L-64, a gentleman who claimed to have visited the prison on a number of occasions, a gentleman who claimed to initially identify the guards as Zenel and Tamuli and changed them, a gentleman who claims that he went to the prison with Dr. Zeqir Gashi. And I'm sure you recall that testimony because he was quite clear about the fact that not only did he visit the prison but he did so in the presence of Dr. Gashi. And Dr. Gashi was there to be of some assistance to an Albanian individual who had been beaten, and Dr. Gashi took the position that he couldn't help and could render no medical assistance. Well, now, if such a thing did occur, then this certainly would be corroborative of a number of things. It certainly would assist L-64's - as it's been suggested - independent ability to tell the truth as long as it didn't relate to him, which I find and I trust the Chamber finds to be a curious way of applying a standard of truth, that I will tell the truth about everybody else but not of myself. That violates almost all rules that we all have grown up with, the simplest one being: To thyself first be true, which means of thyself speak the truth. But with regard to this particular issue, you will remember that Dr. Gashi, when asked the question concerning the prison, specifically said he never went to the prison, never been in the prison. An argument has been put forth here that essentially all witnesses for the Prosecution, that's -- with regard to Dr. Gashi never going to the prison, that's at 5661. With regard to the question in examination-in-chief by Prosecution: "Did you ever visit a prison in Lapusnik?" That's at 5631. His answer is: "No, never." With regard to the issue of those witnesses put forth by the Prosecution, the underlying argument essentially is this: As their testimony relates to our theory of the Prosecution, they are telling the truth. They are truth-tellers. With regard to discrepancies in their testimony, they are either excusable for a variety of reasons, or they're not consequential. Well, the issue about whether or not Dr. Gashi attended the prison with L-64 is something which is relatively central to a number of questions concerning what happened, what is reliable, and who, if either, you choose to believe. Because either L-64 is telling the truth and Dr. Gashi is lying or Dr. Gashi is telling the truth and L-64 is lying. It's one or the other. This isn't a question of mistake. This isn't a question of confusion. And if one of them is lying about something which has not only been put forward as relatively important but also pretty dramatic, a doctor going to place and saying, I can't render any help, then I suggest to you: If they're willing to lie about something that important - and I echo some of the comments that have been made not only in the submissions recently but in the submissions previously - that if they are lying their testimony should be discounted. I have noticed that an argument that's been put forth and a suggestion to you once again with regard to identification is that those witnesses who failed, who did not identify anyone in the photo spread, who did not say in the photo spread that they saw Shala, were either infirm, weak, or had suffered trauma to the extent that they were incapable of giving such information or being able to establish and identify. Well, if one is to take a look behind what is being asked, you're being asked to draw an inference. And if you're being asked to draw an inference, then you're being asked something else. Because inferences arise in the area of circumstantial evidence. Inferences arise with regard to, not cobbling, but putting information together from which you can draw a conclusion. And the importance of the analysis with regard to circumstantial evidence, which is recognised in this jurisdiction and recognised in many jurisdictions, is that if there are two plausible, reasonable explanations, one which leads to guilt and the other which leads to innocence, you must follow that which leads to innocence. That's the path you take. There's a sensible reason for that, because obviously you're balancing. Obviously you've got two competing ideas. And if they both have some form of reasonable credibility to you, well then you haven't met the standard of reasonable doubt. It's a lot -- it's a logical way of doing things and something that I trust, because you're Judges, you've thought of in terms of the way you put the law together because I watch -- it's here. One of the things you're doing is you're creating a law and you're thinking through the way that evidence should be analysed. What happens when you have a variety of different factors put together, what do you do with it? And I'm sure you don't engage in just a rote kind of analysis here, but you carefully choose and weigh. And this situation where you have a suggestion, the suggestion being that these people were too infirm, and it is for that reason that you don't have to give them any credibility with regard to the negative identifications. But you give them definite, positive credibility with regard to an in-dock identification because they were traumatised as opposed to another plausible explanation: It wasn't him. He wasn't there. He's not a dark man. His physical condition is such - and I will speak more about his physical condition - that the kinds of activities they're ascribing to him are not activities that reasonably he could engage in, reasonably he could engage in. Assuming for purposes that you do not accept what you have been told and what we believe to be, because it is, the truth of his situation. Haradin Bala is a sick man, having lived like many of his people, under the boot of the Serbs heard the shots of war, he heard gunshots. And he told you that he went to go fight. He told you that others told him that he should not. And if there's one thing which is consistent in everything that you've heard about Haradin Bala, apart from the fact that he's stubborn, it is that he is sick. You have independent medical records establishing that this man has, for over a decade now, suffered from at least three and perhaps as many as five, depending on how you read the records that have been placed before you under seal, heart attacks. Not a smart thing for a sick man to go fight in a war. He's a young man, too, he's 47 years old. He's a young man now, but he did that. He did what any person in his situation would do: He took his family momentarily to the first point of safety, Nekovce, he then went to go fight. Now to get to Nekovce from where he lives, and examination of the maps will show you, is a checkpoint, Komorane. You can't be walking with a gun through that area. So after taking his family to safety, he went and got his gun and went to Lapusnik. He arrived in Lapusnik some time probably after the fighting, right after the fighting. And he stayed there for a relatively short period of time. So there is no doubt, there's no mistake, we are absolutely in agreement that Haradin Bala was in Lapusnik; that is not a question. The question is when and for how long. Now, the answer to this question, as the evidence has shown, is that he was in Lapusnik until the point in time that Commander Kumanova and he left, which is the end of May. He was seen in Lapusnik during that period of time by Elmi Sopi. He was seen in Lapusnik weakened during that period of time by Dr. Zeqir Gashi. Now, it is important to remember that up until the time of these proceedings Zeqir Gashi was not an anticipated or contemplated witness by the Prosecution. By motion in March, they sought to have him be allowed to testify because he would, as they put it, contest the alibi presented by Mr. Bala. Now, you have before you, it's in evidence, the statement of Mr. Tucker. The statement of Mr. Tucker is DB7 and it involves his interview with Dr. Gashi in which Dr. Gashi, according to Mr. Tucker's interview, notes was operating a clinic in Lapusnik May/June/July 1998 and it started in May or June. Now, Mr. Tucker says that nobody was paying too terribly much attention at that time, they weren't focussing on a date when Dr. Gashi started his medical efforts. And for the moment assuming that is the case and assuming the reason why Dr. Gashi was being called by the Prosecution to testify, one would have thought, considering the discussions that had been had in these proceedings for many months concerning the invisibility of asking leading questions that the following would not have occurred because if indeed this information was both as accurate and as solid as the Prosecution now contends, they would have wanted it to have arisen as pure as the driven snow, not driven to it. Question, 5621: "Did you know anything about Haradin Bala's father?" That's a non-leading question. "Everyone in Drenica knew his father. He was a well-known singer of folk songs. "Q. During June and July of 1998, did you see Haradin Bala in Lapusnik?" "Mr. Guy-Smith: Objection, leading. He can ask him what times he saw him, but he's leading him to an answer at this time. "Mr. Whiting: It's hard, Your Honour, to" -- he didn't get to complete the answer. And I guess if I would ask you to draw an inference, one that leads to guilt, the other that leads to innocence, he would obviously prefer the one of innocence, that it's hard to ask a question and I suggest the proper end to that would be: It's hard to get the answer that I want. I leave that as an aside. "Judge Parker: Just carry on. Whatever harm there is has been done, so --" Now, once the bell has been rung, as we all know, it's not unrung. So now the question is asked again: "Did you see Haradin Bala in Lapusnik?" "Yes." "Q. When did you see him in Lapusnik? "A. He came to our clinic once for a check-up. "Q. But when was it in terms of the time period? "A. When we stayed in Lapusnik. "Q. Can you be more clear?" And the answer comes: "June and July of 1998." Well, I'll be. Gosh, darn. What do you know? There's an example of something that all lawyers fall into, and many Judges criticise us for doing so, which is testify, and we don't get to do that. That's not what this is about. It's not the unblemished response coming from a witness allowing you to make a determination with regard a relatively critical issue for both sides. Now, I'm not suggesting to you here, to be very clear, that Dr. Gashi did anything wrong. I don't think he did. I suggest to you that by asking the question in the fashion that he did, the value of the assertion that Dr. Gashi saw Haradin Bala in June and July of 1998 is worthless, especially in light of the fact that we do know he was operating a clinic and he was engaged in offering medical assistance in Lapusnik during May. And we know that Haradin Bala pretty much visited wherever he could in order to get whatever medical assistance he might, not only during the summer months but before the summer months when he would visit and obtain medication from Ferat Sopi, the man whose home in which Dr. Gashi's medical clinic was operating. Ferat Sopi, a druggist, had been giving Mr. Bala medicine for his condition, his cardiac condition, for years before 1998. During the months of June and July, he was seen by and treated for, to the extent that he could be, his medical condition by Dr. Fetim Selimi, uncontradicted, uncontroverted testimony, unchallenged. Dr. Selimi told you that not on one occasion but on a number of occasions he saw Haradin Bala. He saw his condition. He heard his complaints. He attempted to render medical assistance to him. His condition was that of one who had cardiac difficulties. He was using nitroglycerine, a medicine used for individuals who have cardiac difficulties. His lips on at least one occasion were blue, meaning that he wasn't getting a sufficient amount of oxygenated blood. He was brought there by others because he was not capable of making on his own. It was hot. Dr. Selimi told Haradin Bala, Light duties; go home. The most important thing in once sense that Dr. Selimi told us was that he wouldn't have thought much about Haradin Bala, but he saw him on television in connection with these proceedings. He goes, what's that guy doing there? I know that guy. I treated him. I remember him. I didn't have a lot of people from the KLA coming to me with cardiac problems. Sure, they came to me to be treated for their wounds but not for a cardiac problem. Is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Dr. Selimi saw Haradin Bala during the months of June and July. He saw him in a place which makes it nigh on possible for him, that is Haradin Bala, to have been at Lapusnik. No man, including Haradin Bala, can be in two places as once. During the months of June and July, you have heard evidence from innumerable sources. It was hot. The Prosecution opened its case discussing how rugged the mountains were around Lapusnik area, and Dr. Selimi himself, who commented that at that time - he wasn't commenting about his state of physical health when he testified - but at that time he was in good health. And for him during the year in the summer months of 1998, it was difficult to negotiate those areas, which is something that I will return to in a few moments. It has been suggested that Avdulla Puka, who told you that Haradin Bala stayed with him at his home in Javor, was mistaken or confused because he couldn't remember what he had for dinner last week. Well, Mr. Puka related his memory of Mr. Bala's presence at his home to something that he had been doing for years, because every year he did the same thing: He harvested the grass for his animals. That occurs at a certain time. And for those of us who have spent a moment or two on a farm, you can't cut the grass too early or too late if it does going to be fodder for an animal. Mr. Puka associated Mr. Bala's presence at his home with something with something that he's been doing for years. It's uncontroverted, it's uncontradicted. And there was no motivation that was suggested why Mr. Puka would be lying, mistaken, or otherwise inaccurate. Skender Bylykbashi, once again in speaking about his seeing of Mr. Bala related it to specific events or items of importance, because you will recall he told us that when Haradin Bala came he came with food, he came with flour. And it was the flour that Mr. Bylykbashi was interested in because flour was a substance that he could use to feed those people about him. And he was curious and interested in the availability of the flour. It was not contradicted, it was not refuted, nor were any reasons given or suggested why he should not be believed. Ali Thaqi who has known Haradin Bala all his life told us about his medical condition, a medical condition that we have independent information about. He gave us information about other aspects of his time with Haradin Bala. Not refuted, not contradicted. But you're told that his alibi is a lie. L-64 is a truth-teller; these people are liars. Ferat Sopi, an older man, a man certainly of his own mind as I think we all saw, told us that Dr. Gashi opened his clinic at his home, that he was not sure of the date, that he remembers working with Dr. Gashi, if I'm not mistake, in the latter part of May. Now, there was much conversation concerning what he said and didn't say in an unrecorded conversation with Prosecution over whether or not what he read -- whatever he did read in Koha Ditore with regard to Dr. Gashi's testimony was accurate, as contended by the Prosecution, meaning he said he read all of the testimony and it was accurate. That is the inference you are to draw because there is never any information which is clear as to whether or not the man even read the entirety of the testimony. But be that as it may, he said, that is Ferat Sopi, that he didn't tell them it was entirely accurate. He said there were some problems with it. Now, the article itself, which is in evidence and which was discussed during his examination, also has in it the date of May and also has in it the fact that the date of May related to when Dr. Zeqir Gashi was running the clinic. Now, I pause and go somewhere else for a moment. Curious, strange, I suggest, especially in light of these proceedings, especially in light of the difficulties that the Prosecution ostensibly was having with certain witnesses that in dealing with the interview of somebody like Dr. -- I'm sorry, Ferat Sopi, who was once again critical on an issue of time and place concerning the whereabouts of Mr. Bala, and specifically concerning his assertion that he was not in Lapusnik; curious that such an interview was not tape recorded or video recorded, so he, like others, could be declared hostile if such a statement was made. Now, if we had been given this from the outset, from the very beginning of the case, before the kinds of things that had happened here, I would not make such a suggestion. But considering the manner in which such a powerful tool, which they have suggested it is, and such an absolute tool which they have suggested it is, because you could see the mannerisms, you could hear the words, you as the triers of fact would have before you each and every breath of that interview so you could judge what was said, is not before you. In order for you to find that Haradin Bala on July 25th, fall of Lapusnik, walked up the mountain in the heat of the day an area rugged, defined by a number of individuals, you necessarily have to discount the testimony of Dr. Selimi. You have to discount the testimony even of Dr. Gashi with regard to Haradin Bala's physical condition because one of the things that you were told specifically by Dr. Selimi was -- during the period of time that he saw Haradin Bala - and now for the moment I'm going to make a theoretical jump and he saw Haradin Bala and that Haradin Bala somehow got back to Lapusnik, an area which would be virtually impossible to get to, and he went back up the mountain - all of which, I contend, and I don't believe the evidence has shown at all - that he was having difficulty breathing; that he was having difficulty moving step by step in the heat of the summer, something that you have heard was a constant in his life. Now, I ask you here to draw an inference if you choose to reject what we contend we have proven, that he was not at Lapusnik. There is no doubt, it has been proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that Haradin Bala suffered a physical condition of some gravity. You have heard evidence that his physical condition during this time - I won't say was fragile - but certainly was not good, that he was incapable of doing that which a normal man his age or older - and those are words that I use - would do. Now, remember, because now you have been told not once but a number of times by the Prosecution that Haradin Bala is the man who beat people. Not once or twice, a little wrap on the wrist, but we're talking about some good floggings, 59 times at one point in time, one gentleman testified to. Now, I ask you: If in fact the individual who did that was Haradin Bala, how was he physically capable of doing it? How? If his situation was such that he was having difficulty breathing while perambulating, the kind of effort it would take to wield a stick for that period of time is not something that, I suggest to you, he could have done. Now, in our opening we said we cannot say he was incapable of it because we can't. We do not evidence that says he was incapable of it, but I do suggest to you here we have clear circumstantial evidence, clear evidence from which you can reasonably, logically, and objectively draw an inference. And the inference to be drawn is that based upon his recognised physical condition - testified to by many, recorded up to this very day - he was not a man he was capable of engaging in those activities. But I take it for a moment even a step to the side, not further but to the side. Because you have in your possession statements made by, I believe, two gentlemen, L-04 and L-06. Those statements are statements which, as you know, per agreement, received after both of these gentlemen testified, statements which were given to Serbian authorities concerning their experiences. L-04's statement was given on the 1st of October, 1998. It's P203, I believe. It's either 203 or 204, but I look to Mr. Younis, as we all do, to make sure that I'm not misrepresenting the record. 203. Now, L-04 has testified that going up the mountain there that Shala was one of the people who went up there. Now, we have been given a series of excuses for why information would be either incorrect or, in this instance, people would not wish to admit they had anything to do with the Serbs because it would be impolitic. And their denial of any statements made to the Serbs is understandable, apart from the fact that these statements themselves are in fact laden. I refer for the Court's review the following paragraph, paragraph 10, in which L-04 relates the following: "After a month spent in the prison, the source states he was taken out of the room together with," some other people. "They then blindfolded them and drove them in a passenger vehicle to Kishna Reka where there were other people who had been kidnapped by the KLA. The kidnapped individuals were surrounded by eight KLA members in camouflage uniform and masks on their heads." Now, we know, everybody has agreed, that a number of individuals, many individuals wore masks. They wore masks to not be identified. And that is the first information given concerning L-04's release. L-06, which I believe is 204, with regard to his release states: "After a month in prison the source said they were taken out to the doorway of the room where they were being kept, that sacks were placed over their heads and they were then taken to Kishna Reka village, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gllogovc, where the sacks were removed." Names no one with regard to identity. Says he saw his brother and others for the first time. But then, importantly, because a suggestion has been made that part of the reason that these individuals were reluctant to discuss any of this was because they didn't want to have any information go back where it could be determined or assume that they had anything to do with the Serbs, so that they would not ever identify anybody who they might have been able to identify in the KLA - assuming they could - this gentleman says: "At the end of the interview the source stated that amongst the KLA members," and he says who kidnapped him and some others, "he recognised," and then he gives a series of names. The name "Shala" does not appear. The name "Haradin Bala" does not appear. We do know that in a certain sense this is a small community, and we have heard from some, including L-96, that whispers brought names, that people talked, and that names were then attributed to other names. And upon those kinds of correlations, a guess being made, as is suggested, highly speculative, not particularly reliable, there is no foundation. You're asked to assume on a whisper that the information is accurate, that he became convinced that Shala was Haradin Bala. But the evidence, if examined closely and objectively, establishes that it is speculative in nature and does not bear sufficient indicia of reliability to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Bala was involved in these activities. Memory's a curious thing, and a person's desire to resolve a trauma, make sure that that which happened to them historically is satisfied, I think we all know, we have seen on more than one occasion, can push towards conclusions that are not substantiated by the actual evidence produced. It is easy to say in the most emotional of senses that we have proved our case beyond all possible doubt, which has been said to you by the Prosecution repeatedly in their final submission. And what should give you pause is that they do not take into account the independent, external, objective information that could cast doubt and refute it. They do not in their advocacy give you the complete picture and say, Looking at the totality of the circumstances which we, by virtue of our position as Prosecutors must do responsibly by taking into account what we acknowledge are areas that you should be concerned about if indeed this is a search for the truth, and having taking all of that into account, Your Honours, we say to you that we have satisfied our burden -- that they did not do. They shy away from those difficulties. And the reason that they shy away from those difficulties is because those very points establish that which they choose not to confront: Their failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. Their failure for you to be comfortable having the surgery I suggested to you at the beginning. Because once you begin to question the doctors - and now I suggest you take each and every witness and place them in the operating theatre, assign them whatever task you will: attending nurse, assistant anaesthesiologist, assistant surgeon, and you put them in that theatre - and you have the opportunity to ask them the questions that you would ask before going under the knife, you would not be satisfied. You would home for a miracle. You would look for another form of treatment. Haradin Bala's a simple man. He comes to you from a somewhat different tradition than others before you might have. As I said earlier, he too, as all seem to have in Kosovo, suffered under the boot of Serbian oppression. He told you that -- when he spoke with you that a mistake had been made. He told you that when he heard these things he felt sad. Now, I believe that there is at this time insufficient evidence and a failure by the Prosecution and that is verdict that you should render in this case objectively is one of not guilty. I had not intended on commenting at all with regard to issues concerning sentencing. I find it actually to be, as an advocate, inappropriate and awkward to do so. I have been concerned about this because also as an advocate I wish never to waive any rights that attach to my client. So I have this to say: If after a careful consideration of all the evidence, if after an analysis when engaging in those areas where inferences are to be drawn, which is perhaps where you may spend a fair amount of time in your deliberations, you make the determination that he was involved in these activities, any or all, you obviously will then have another duty to perform. He has told you about his family, he has told you who he is. And I started off by saying he is a simple man, who probably in a very real sense - you've seen some of the reports, you've read some of the medical reports - his time is more limited than most. How much longer, I don't know. That he has repeated medical difficulties does seem to be true. What they are have not yet been diagnosed. They seem to have taken care of certain aspects of his heart, thank goodness; there are other things going on and the records you have before you establish that. His contributions to the world of the future are simple ones, really. He looks forward to, as he told you, a society where all of the boys and girls play together. He won't be a politician. He won't negotiate. He won't do many of the things that other fine human beings will do and one has done. But he will live his life out, whatever that is remaining, in, I believe, a quiet and dignified fashion. He would never appear before any Tribunal of any sort. He would not be here today had he not heard the gunshots, had he not decided to go fight for his people, had he listened to the pleas of his family, which is, Haradin, you're too sick, you're too old, you don't belong doing these kinds of things. But he did not. So whatever choices you would make in that regard, if you reach that point - which I suggest to you you won't and you shouldn't after analysis of all the information - is a very insubstantial period, if any at all. Thank you for your consideration. I trust my remarks did not offend, and I hope that they have given you the appropriate basis upon which to consider the task which lays before you of determining this gentleman's fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. We begin this closing speech, the last you will hear, by recalling the opening lines of another. This was delivered by Robert Jackson, who was at the time an associate justice of the United States Supreme Court. But as he spoke these words, he was lead counsel for the Prosecution, standing now some 60 years ago before the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg when he said this: "An advocate can be confronted with few more formidable tasks than to select his closing arguments, where there is a great disparity between his appropriate time and his available material." Well, it's been, by my calculation, 87 days that you have been hearing and receiving, in oral and documentary form, a huge amount of detailed evidence. So what shall we do? Well, we will attempt, precocious as it may be, to do precisely that which Justice Jackson attempted to do 60 years ago, to lift this case out of the morass of detail and put before you, sometimes only in summary form, occasionally in a little more substance, the bold outlines of the case for and on behalf of Isak Musliu. What's our purpose? Well, our purpose is three-fold: first of all, to highlight and comment upon what we consider to be the main points for and against him, as set out in the final briefs of both sides; secondly, to demonstrate how and why this jury of jurists can and should find that the case against him has failed; thirdly, to demonstrate that that failure has come about because in respect of each and every count on this indictment, there is either no evidence or, such as there is, either taken alone or with other evidence, is either unreliable or suffers from inherent weakness or is contradicted by other evidence so as to render this entire case against Isak Musliu fatally flawed. Bold claims. Justifiable ones, we submit. A mountain to climb? We shall see. Can we make, please, in the hope that they make assist, some general introductory remarks. Can we begin where an English judge could begin any summing up to an English jury, where the Prosecution begin at paragraph 293 on their section on law and application mirrored in paragraph 26 of the joint Defence briefs: "The burden and standard of proof are familiar enough," encapsulated, of course, as they are in Article 21's presumption of innocence. You must be sure of two things: First of all, that the crimes charged have been committed; and secondly, that the accused whose case you are considering, and I underline those words, is beyond reasonable doubt responsible for those crimes. May I pass to a word on functions. Now that we've reached a closing stage at this case, the elision in this jurisdiction between your functions of judges of law and fact as well as your powers and your duties to regulate and supervise this trial process do, in a very real sense, turn Your Honours into a jury of jurists, which of course is not yet familiar to us in the United Kingdom, but it will be soon. It's familiar to you all from your own jurisdictions, of course. But you're not, as it's been observed more than once in the last 87 days, a raw jury. You're not amateur debutants in the process, professional judges appointed as such. And in a very real sense your joint and several tasks in reaching a judgement in this case may be harder than if you were a lay jury of 12, directed in the law by a professional judge. How so harder? Harder, perhaps, to allay the fear and suspicion that you may be less than willing to apply the standard and burden of proof. It is or may be harder to demonstrate to a lay defendant or to the lay public looking on how it is, for example, that you are able to receive and hear evidence and give it little or no weight or even reject it and then move on. The lay jury receives only that which the professional judge permits them to hear, excluding from them, where possible, the irrelevant, the immaterial, and the prejudicial. This jury hears it all, or most of it. And that is why we say to an onlooker, to a defendant, the task for you may seem more difficult. No wonder then the public or a defendant may have doubts and require assurance and reassurance that fairness and open-mindedness prevails to the end of the process. In this very case at the very beginning of it, our client, through us, as did others in this dock, voice concerns and fears, which for our client and indeed the others was overcome by them, to place their faith and their futures in the hands of this Chamber and this process as being a fair one. But, Your Honours, fairness is not weakness. If this Chamber comes to the decisions we argue for in the case of Isak Musliu, then it will have, we suggest, resoundingly demonstrated the true meaning, the true power of the principle that guilt can only be established if you and each of you is satisfied so that you are sure of it. It may well be that in this case of Isak Musliu where rarely, as we understand it in the jurisprudential history of this Tribunal, a defendant gives or calls no live evidence that this principle receives its sternest test. A word on your approach, if we may. Evaluating or assessing the evidence is dealt with, of course, in both side's briefs. May we suggest a shorthand approach. Decide first on the evidence you can be sure of in relation to the issue you are considering and your inferences from and only from that evidence. Assessing witnesses, the questions that of course will be posed. Have they come to assist, to speak the truth? Have they come driven by other less noble motives? Is their testimony wholly unaffected by others? In our opening we also invited you to consider the possibility, if at all, of the extent to which, if at all, old scores, old enmities were or may be being settled. Can we turn to another area, again by way of introduction, again we hope only to assist. When it comes to considering the evidence of that trio who you found to be hostile, Buja, Behluli, Karpuzi, and where the issue of prior statements being taken as substantive arises, we crystallise our submission in two ways: If not believed on their oath before you, they should not be believed at all. On corroboration and corroborative evidence, we suggest and we submit that the only fair and safe way to proceed is to search for evidence in relation to key witnesses such as 64 and 96, which is wholly independent of them. Can we turn from there to a critically important category of evidence in this trial, that of identification. In 28 paragraphs over 13 pages in their final brief, the Prosecution argue that the identifications by witnesses in this case and the procedures adopted to obtain them are reliable. Whether, whether, they were having any unconscious second thoughts regarding procedural rectitude I'll leave to this Chamber to decide. But in doing so, may we point out that in paragraph 151 of their brief, the photo spread identifications and procedures used in all the identifications are submitted to be: "Very reliable." By paragraph 152, they are described as: "Reliable." By paragraph 154 they become "adequate." Reliability for the Prosecution seems to be predicated on the following: First of all, that witnesses heard pseudonyms being spoken; secondly, that witnesses heard the true identities of a defendant via others. For example, L-04 was told that Qerqizi equals Musliu by Milaim Kamberi. So they confidently submit based on that kind of material that, and I quote them: "The victims' knowledge of pseudonyms of the accused while at the camp is strong evidence of their presence there." Well, in the example we've just given that L-04's knowledge is based upon a hearsay statement from an identified source who they could have called but did not call cannot, we submit, provide strong evidence of anything, least of all a positive identification. The Prosecution in support of reliability also submit the victims provide "largely accurate descriptions." Well, that will be, of course, for you to decide. But they make a bold submission in paragraph 140 when they say this in their brief: "Vojko Bakrac described a man fitting Musliu's description as a well-built young man, shorter with the witness, darker haired with a beard." Well, let's go on for a moment in this one example and look at what this witness went on to say about this man who was beating Genov, who fits the description of Isak Musliu, paragraph 140 of their brief. Turn back 14 paragraphs and you'll see them say in their brief, exactly matching Musliu's description. In closing yesterday it becomes "closely matching" the description of Musliu. But what did he go on to say, Bakrac, at page 1.307? "Q. Did this person ever say anything to you about his education or background?" "A." -- this is supposed to be Musliu -- "Afterwards he studied at the university. He'd attended the PE school and he knew martial arts." Three points, Your Honours, we'll hear a little while later on in this speech from L-64 about another man who knew karate in this camp. I'll keep the Tribunal in suspense as to who that is. Secondly, references to a university and PE school do not and cannot refer to Isak Musliu. This is supposed to be the same Musliu who you will recall, according to others, habitually wore a mask and is apparently giving a personal biography to a potential identifying witness. This is not, we suggest, a description fitting of Isak Musliu so you can reliably sure of it, sufficient to find beyond reasonable doubt that he is here to be identified as Isak Musliu and no other. Prosecution submit that L-96 makes a positive identification of Musliu in "extremely favourable conditions." He doesn't. He makes a positive recognition of Musliu, a man he says he knew. Curious if true that Musliu chooses to be unmasked in front of someone who knows him, but that's by the bye. They go on then to make a breathtaking submission as far as L-96 is concerned: "There is no reason for L-96 to be untruthful about having seen Musliu at the prison." Well, we shall see if there are no reasons. Then, submits the Prosecution, the procedures, the photo spreads, and so on are reliable, having been properly and fairly prepared and deployed. May we make six short points on that submission. First of all, may we respectfully ask that the Chamber reminds itself of the cross-examination of Kereakes in order to begin to test that proposition; secondly, may we respectfully remind the Tribunal that identification evidence must be treated with caution, we are going to submit, extreme caution, for we submit you can read extreme caution into the judgement in Kunarac et al.: "Many difficulties inherent in the identification process resulting from the vagaries of human perception and recollection." As an English judge would say: "An honest witness may be a mistaken one. More than one can be both convincing and mistaken. And mistakes can also be made in recognition of someone known, even of a close friend or relative." We do invite this Tribunal to proceed with extreme caution when assessing this category of evidence. We commend Professor Wagenaar's report to you, and in particular his rules. They are, we submit, both modest and sensible. And we remind, finally, sixthly, this Tribunal in general terms regarding purported identifications of Isak Musliu that the position is simply as follows: He was only identified by being recognised by L-26. He's been identified by no one else. He was not identified by L-12. He was picked out of a photo spread by L-64 -- hardly a surprise, a KLA man who knew him. L-04 was confronted with a picture by Kereakes who used photo board U1 -- I think that may be the one that went missing, I'm not sure - to which L-04 said, Well, he looked familiar but I'm not sure. Isak Musliu is in a unique position in this trial. There is no identification of him by anyone, and all there is a purported recognition by L-96. The Prosecution finally and perhaps somewhat unusually submit in paragraph 157 of their brief that the dock identifications in this case, and I quote them again: "Provide strong corroboration of the other evidence showing the presence of the accused in the prison." Two points: If that is intended to include Isak Musliu, there was no in-court identification of him, I remind you; Hardly surprising, you may think. Secondly, the Prosecution's submission has to be placed alongside the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. I pick another example in Tadic where the Tribunal explicitly stated they would place little or no reliance on it, the "it" being the dock identification, and they would assess the credibility of each witness independently of it. And they go on in that same paragraph, 157, of their brief, again to make another bold submission, bearing in mind one aspect of this case that we have from time to time raised in cross-examination. They say this: "The victims have a strong interest in ensuring that the correct individuals and not simply those on trial are held responsible." No argument with that. "Therefore, it is expected that some, if not all, of the victims who testified, would have alerted the Tribunal in court if the wrong persons were on trial." Well, I just have two words to say in response to that: Agim Murtezi. Not one witness whom we asked took any step whatsoever to tell anyone in the world that the wrong man was here in this dock. The tragic disaster of misidentification, therefore, has occurred in this very case, in the case of the innocent Agim Murtezi. There can be no better way of concluding our submissions on this vital topic than by stealing from the poet Yeats: The ghost of Agim Murtezi bangs upon the door. I'll provide the identity of the person Yeats referred to if required by anyone later. From the practices and procedures adopted to the difficulties we've sought to identify, the identification evidence, such as it is in the case in general and in the case of Musliu in particular, is not very reliable nor reliable nor even adequate. It doesn't exist. So that concludes, again we hope of some assistance, by way of introduction some of the key areas you will be concerned with in terms of your approach to reaching a judgement in his case with one rather special exception, and may I make it lastly in this section. It's not been said by anyone yet, I don't think. There are three defendants on trial, three separate trials, we submit, heard together for obvious reasons of convenience and economy, but three cases nonetheless. Separate defendants demand and require separate consideration and separate verdicts. A finding for or against one does not, cannot, and will not inevitably lead to a finding for or against another. So we can move on to deal with the next aspect of the trial. This was going to be quite a long section, but in the light of the submissions made to you by Mr. Mansfield and the document which we respectfully support having gone in, I wanted to deal at some length with armed conflict and crimes against humanity. But happily, I don't have to. Save, I want to say one thing on armed conflict.
