And may I just remind the Trial Chamber, of course armed conflict relates to the even-numbered counts, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. The strength of the FRY forces relied upon by the Prosecution in support of their arguments does not, we suggest, provide the support they claim that it does. As I understand their submissions, they say that in and of itself the deployment and numerical and logistical strength of the FRY forces shows incontrovertibly, they submit, the nature and extent of the threat posed, and hence, they submit, if I've understood them properly, powerful evidence going to the intensity of the conflict. We say in response to that that the size and deployment of the FRY forces also indicates something else altogether, that there was a different purpose than taking on and defeating such KLA forces as there were at the time you are concerned with. The further, the greater, and we suggest the dominant FRY forces in the spring and summer and autumn and winter of 1998 was nothing more nor less than the ethnic cleansing of Kosovo. That is or may be why such-used forces were engaged, to satisfy the dual purpose of ethnic cleansing as its primary purpose and, at the same time, putting down in the late spring and summer - their words, not mine - "the terrorist KLA." As far as crimes against humanity are concerned, the odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9, again may we respectfully suggest that a definition of crimes against humanity may be helpful to remember, and it comes from Tadic. And I quote: "Crimes against humanity are crimes which by their magnitude and savagery or by their large number or by the fact a similar pattern was applied," and here are the vital words we suggest, "endangered the international community or shocked the conscience of mankind." You will bear in mind the numbers involved here of disappeared, no greater on any estimate than 300. You will set that against the tens of hundreds of thousands of Kosovar Albanians who were displaced and worst. May we make under point under the general head of crimes against humanity, an issue rubbished by the Prosecution more than once in what, if I may say so, was Mr. Whiting's powerful submissions. Susanne Ringaard Petersen, producing OSCE reports did, I repeat, did speak of the existence and the operation of rogue elements - their witness, not ours - which the KLA she said in her reports were found difficult to control involving instances of personal revenge and the like. If Your Honours note, cross-referencing Defence brief paragraph 400. We suggest that when one carefully considers the meaning given in this Tribunal's jurisprudence to term such as widespread and systematic in Akajezu [phoen] for example and the word in Blaskic, for example, then the Prosecution case perhaps begins to unravel just ever so slightly. The ICC Statute, interestingly, makes the existence of a policy rather more fundamental than it is elsewhere. So as far as you are concerned, it would appear that while not a requirement for crimes against humanity, nonetheless we would submit the search should be for the policy as a necessary and important but not essential component. So necessary and important is the way we put it. And therefore, we would submit, to give full effect to that definition, if it's a definition that you are prepared to accept, the search should be for a policy that does take matters beyond the isolated, uncoordinated, and the haphazard. And there is, for assistance in this regard, a stark and clear evidential contrast existing in this case to demonstrate both the absence and the presence of the kind of policy that we have been referring to. Taking the Prosecution's case at its highest, compare and contrast, if you would, we submit, the position as between the KLA on the one hand and what I'll generically refer to as the Serb forces, the instrument of the Serb state, the office of state security, call it what you will, as it were; and the latter being populated - we would say infested - by characters such as Jasevic and Sparavalo. Take into account, if you would, we respectfully submit, our 92 bis material. Read again the statement of K-05. There you will find the existence of a policy. There you will find the practice of a policy to commit crimes against humanity. DM2, the ECMM report, an incident on the 4th of August 1998, the forces of Serb law and order, police officers were burning Albanian houses. Why do you burn someone's house? You burn someone's house to rid them of a home. You burn someone's house to ethnically cleanse your world from them. That is a policy in practice. We suggest it's a comparison that is both helpful and worth making. We can move on to consider under various headings other aspects of the Prosecution's case. So this heading, if you will, is the Prosecution evidence as it relates to Isak Musliu. But before looking at that, may I just stop on the way, as it were, and make a point, a single point, on the indictment. The Trial Chamber will already have noted and will perhaps have noted with interest that it has never been separately alleged in any count on this indictment to which Isak Musliu has pleaded or has been invited to plead that he is alleged to have been charged -- or is charged with the mountain -- the murder in the Berisa Mountains, Counts 9 and 10. He is not and he never has been. So let's look, if we may, please, before the next break at the first area where Isak Musliu features. Your Honours, may I indicate what I'm hoping to achieve here. I'm hoping that should you be bothered to want to look at a transcript of this speech later you might be able to put it alongside the Prosecution's final brief and go through their headings and see, I hope in crystallised form, how we respond to each of them by way of a distillation of and I hope a little amplification of, where appropriate, that which we set out at some length in our written final brief. That is its purpose. We hope it goes some way to serving that purpose. So where do we start? The Prosecution's pick up the cudgels, if that word can be translated, under the heading of Limaj's area of responsibility. And they set out a number of matters in that heading in that part of their brief. What I want to light upon is only one, I think. Maybe two, but certainly one. They quote from Isak Musliu's diary at paragraph 22 and they use that in support of the existence of a KLA structure. By virtue of Musliu's reference to training on arrival being "designated tasks and pseudonyms," it's apparent, they say, and I quote them, paragraph 22, that "already by this time in April 1998, Limaj was known as Commander Celiku." Well, may I please simply invite the Tribunal to look at the transcript, not now but later, page 502 to 505, and may I also please invite the Tribunal if it thinks there's any teeth in the Prosecution's submission about this diary to look at the diary itself. It's Exhibit P4. You will see and you will note that the diary is not alike a diary that any of us may have in our pockets, at least in the form that's before us here; it goes forwards and backwards. And the passages that they quote from to make the emphatic point they make is headed a "delayed diary." You'll see a date in June, the 11th, and the next entry is June the 2nd. Your Honours, there's been no evidence regarding this diary, other than it being produced by way of commentary, as it were, by Mr. Lehtinen when he gave evidence at the very beginning of this trial. Yet - yet - this warrants comments about it in paragraph 22 of the Prosecutor's brief that it is clear and it is apparent and plainly. Well, we submit, not so. Beware the confident assertion, which here is we suggest without any evidential basis whatsoever regarding this diary. Also relied upon -- there was one other matter on this heading of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Limaj's areas of responsibility, one other matter I did want to deal with very briefly indeed, because also relied upon under this head by the Prosecution is a matter that will, I suspect, exercise you more than the diary, and that is the establishment of the 121st Brigade on the 6th of August, 1998, or thereabouts, which, it is suggested, merely as it were formalised an already existing structure. Well, there is, we suggest, sufficient evidence emanating from former KLA witnesses when added to by Crosland and Churcher to suggest that far from being a continuum the formation of the brigade and its development was a response, a response to the significant defeats in July and the significant defects identified in the structure in organisation prior to July. The component parts may have existed, but the structure, we submit, did not until post-August. I was here going to use a cricketing analogy, but I understand that cricket may be a painful subject for at least one member of this Tribunal as I stand here as an Englishman this afternoon, so I'll use a football analogy. The coach may have had a squad of players, but the team and its substitutes was not picked to fight what became a very different game post-August than the one that had been engaged upon prior to August. Mr. Powles has written the word "break now" in his notebook. Can Your Honours indicate when the next one is to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It could happen now or in the next 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed. Resuming at 10 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: One comment and two corrections. The comment is if I didn't make clear that as I read the Musliu diary, all entries as are written appear to relate to 1999. Second point is that his diary is P23 and not P4. And perhaps more important than any of that, of course I did not mean to say that it's only the even counts to which armed conflict applies; armed conflict of course applies to the entirety of the indictment. May I move on to deal, please, with the next heading as it appears in the Prosecution's brief, and that is titled "the KLA in Lapusnik." The evidence seems to be that converging on Lapusnik from a variety of different towns and villages came, initially at least, handfuls of men, uncoordinated and without direct leadership. In a ruling that Your Honours gave on the application regarding the witness Behluli and in seeking to summarise his, the witness's, position, with apparent approval the Trial Chamber at transcript page 2.740, described the position prior to the formation of brigades in this way: "Small, volunteer groups or points which operated in isolation from each other or in cooperation only by mutual agreement." We respectfully adopt that as an accurate characterisation of the position, certainly in the spring, if not in the early summer, of 1998. The Prosecution of course would have it and make it very clear that they would have it that it was far more structured and organised than that. Of course amongst these groups that converge on Lapusnik was one containing, it would seem, L-64 and Fadil Kastrati, led to Lapusnik by Alushani and his Zari [phoen] group. This was, it seems, according to L-64, the same group, some of whose members were in the escort business. The Prosecution assert in effect that the 9th of May saw the permanent and secure establishment of the KLA in Lapusnik, which we submit was, as further battles showed over the next weeks, anything but secure. For, within 12 weeks or so they were of course ousted. To the Prosecution no longer was the KLA here about hit-and-run, but they were about securing and holding a strategically important area. So it is that Celiku 3 is born, fighting positions are established, units and shifts recorded in notebooks, an HQ is established, roadblocks are established and so on. A source, some may say the main source, of the evidence touching on these matters, at least before you, comes from no less a quarter of honesty, truth, and reliability than L-64 himself. From him comes notebooks, from him digging trenches, creating firing positions, from him evidence regarding the HQ. From him, but not only him, evidence regarding rules. From him, evidence of Musliu's power to discipline and so on and so forth. Another source of some of that material of course is Ruzhdi Karpuzi, a witness declared hostile by Your Honours. May we have a word or two now on him. Karpuzi told you in cross-examination the following: He got a uniform in December of 1998; he got to Lapusnik by tractor and by foot; he was the one who placed tabs on the plan or one of those who placed tabs on the plan to show positions; he said Voglushi was elected one of the leaders and then Qerqiz: "We asked Voglushi to become a leader for us. Qerqiz was not elected to become the one and only commander in Lapusnik," he said. I tried as best as I could in cross-examination to, as it were, nail that down. "Q. I suggest Qerqiz was elected to become the leader of one of the units in Lapusnik. "A. You are right." He was at position number 1; who was his leader there? Last name Zogi, pseudonym Mjeshtri. He kept records of soldiers. He told you, it was absurd to suggest, as L-64 had, that he kept records of prisoners. Qerqizi sang in the oda in the compound; hardly, as Your Honours may think, evidence designed to assist Musliu, assuming he was hostile to the Prosecution. But that of course is a matter for you upon which you have ruled. Went no where else in the compound did this witness, apart from the oda. The Prosecution of course would have it that everyone who walked through those gates knew or must have known what was happening within them. And may we observe this on the application to turn this witness hostile: There were four bases for it, or rather four topics on which the Prosecution relied, as we understand the transcript and recollect the argument. They were as to the oath ceremony and Mr. Limaj being a leader; it was as to seeing Mr. Limaj in Lapusnik; it was as for Mr. Limaj being called Celiku; and it was as matters regarding Shala. Therefore, the application did not involve anything regarding all he'd said up to that point concerning Musliu or structure or organisation, which corresponded to what he agreed in cross-examination by us. Beyond Karpuzi, upon whom in these respects you can rely, we are as we suggested for the most of the remainder of the incriminating material under this head, looking to L-64. Let's be clear. There were trenches and firing positions, of course there were; there were notebooks kept, of course there were; there were diaries; there may well have been places and were places we now call HQ; there were moments requiring some sort of disciplinary action - we put one as part of our case in cross-examination to L-64. But there is, we say, no clear nor reliable evidence that Musliu either was or performed sufficient acts to demonstrate that he was in anything like the position the Prosecution claimed for him. And what is that position? They make it now very clear, I underline the word "now," the commander in Lapusnik and in the camp. That is now their case which logically brings me to their next heading: "The camp in Lapusnik." Four matters are relied on here in support of the assertion that there was a camp in Lapusnik. Witnesses recognised its environs, the area; documents found post-July 26. L-96 and his return there with Jasevic. And Buja's evidence regarding L-07. Paragraph 29 of the Defence pre-trial brief states our position, we submit, very clearly. We submit, we hope with equal clarity, that our position has not changed. Our duty, as we perceive it, has been to test, explore, and examine the Prosecution's case. We have positively asserted by calling no other evidence no other case. We have called no evidence on this or any other point. Our position remains unchanged. If there was such a place, Isak Musliu was not involved in it or with it. The role of the accused in Lapusnik and the camp. Here we'll divide it up in two parts, the command role and the role of individual responsibility. Can I deal first then with the command role as pleaded. The case here of course is that Musliu was Limaj's subordinate commander. There is no real dispute at trial, say the Prosecution at paragraph 117, that Musliu was the commander of Celiku 3 in Lapusnik. Your Honours, in the light of Mr. Fatmir's evidence to that very effect, it does not lie in my mouth to argue with that, but I can assure Your Honours that there is a real dispute that Musliu was the commander at Lapusnik as opposed to a commander. And we are not here seeking to dance on the head of a pin. There was more than one unit in or around Lapusnik. There was no, we submit, overall commander. There was not a commander by the name of Qerqizi in overall command of that village. I hope that makes it clear. Here we rely on something that the Prosecution in its speech pours scorn upon. We rely on Musliu's own description of his own role in that extremely important interview of his dated the 24th of May of 2001. This, say the Prosecution in closing, is an interview that contains deliberate lies. We submit not. But why is it that we give it the title "extremely important"? May I develop our reasons. This was Musliu being interviewed as a witness, not as a suspect. He was alone without any representation. This was nearly two years before he was arrested. You may think we would positively invite you to find the following six things about this interview: one, when interviewed he would have had no reason to feel under suspicion; two, he was at the time of the interview a serving police officer, to he may be taken to know and to appreciate the importance of where he was and what he was being asked; three, he would, you may safely conclude, at that point know nothing of international humanitarian law, and in particular nothing like enough about the complexities of armed conflict or crimes against humanity to be able to be cagey or worse when asked about what position he held; fourth, in plain English he could not know that four years down the line the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal would seek to portray him as a commander; fifth, he would not, you may think, have been alert nor particularly on his guard, for he would have had no reason to be; sixth, you may conclude, therefore, that he gives here in this interview an honest and accurate answer and one which - and how, Your Honours, could he possibly know this? - chimes in with the very position he now takes: I was a team leader; I was one of others; I was not the commander for all; there were other units and other commanders. What else do the Prosecution rely upon to suggest that Musliu was the commander? L-64, the position 1 logbook showing an apparent visit by Ambassador Hill speaking to a Commander Qerqiz at 4.00 on the 26th of June, 1998, to be exact. Dr. Gashi's evidence and Fatmir Limaj, of course, saying that he was the commander of Celiku 3. Put all those together, say the Prosecution, and you have powerful evidence he was the commander. Well, let's deal with these in turn. L-64 said he did not know if Qerqizi had arrested or given orders to arrest, but only he knew he could enter the prison, which he saw him do, he says, on two or three occasions. How did he put it, L-64? Transcript 4847: "My opinion about him is that he was a commander, but I'm not saying he was in charge of the prison or that he had any responsibilities but he was a commander above the soldiers there, that is true." L-96 is worth remembering as the only other witness who gives evidence about Musliu's involvement in the camp. Ramiz Qeriqi said this, 3.595: Musliu "could have been a platoon commander in charge of 20 soldiers, not more;" possible. I'm not accurate. "Commander of a platoon." When Fadil Kastrati in around June or July sought permission to leave Lapusnik, he was, we submit, not clear who the right person was to speak to. When he did finally speak to Qerqiz it was rather more of a discussion or a consultation than Qerqiz actually giving him permission. For Your Honours' note, transcript 2.610 to 11. Byslym Zyrapi visited Lapusnik in May and June. On one of three visits, the commander of Lapusnik, he said, introduced himself. What was his name? Voglushi. Transcript 6826. That of course doesn't get a mention by the Prosecution at all. Shukri Buja spoke of a commander for each of several units. He implied, you may think, that Qerqiz or Voglushi were in charge of Lapusnik but he was also, you may think, somewhat ambiguous about it. But in any event, in any event, any business - you may remember the word - Buja had he seems to have conducted with Voglushi. On that, he was clear. But he was not entirely clear, we submit, as to who overall, if anyone, commanded. Well, the Prosecution nonetheless, uninhibited as they are, bold as they are, go on to submit in brief and orally that Voglushi Alushani was a deputy commander regarded by some as a leader. Well, I don't know where the evidence is for that. They seem to think it's here. It's not a case I've heard if I may respectfully submit. Logbook 1 and this visit by the ambassador. May I simply say this about it: Its provenance, accuracy, has not for the purposes of this point been sufficiently or at all, still less satisfactorily, aired to entitle the Prosecution, in our submission, to make such an emphatic point about it. No evidence has been given, none, as to where, when, and in what circumstances this entry was placed in the book. Dr. Gashi did say, did day, that he understood Qerqiz to be the leader of the KLA in Lapusnik. That is true. But he was cross-examined and in that cross-examination did importantly concede, you may think, that he had no personal knowledge in fact about who commanded the KLA. And finally, and importantly, and we do not seek to step around it or through it or underneath it or over it, Mr. Limaj made clear that Mr. Musliu was or became the commander of Celiku 3. Your Honours, he was, as we have been at pains to remind you, clear that there were other units at and in Lapusnik, Guri and Pellumbi. And indeed on the 25th of July battle, that wasn't all, for Mr. Limaj was to tell you at page 6.539 that as it were elements of Celiku 1 and 2 also participated in the fighting at that time. So where are we on this important topic of Musliu's role, his command role, it is said both in Lapusnik and in the camp? Well, our comments and our submissions are set out under various heads between paragraphs 1.008 and 1.035 in our brief. No witness we have been considering claims that Musliu was the commander responsible for crimes within a prison or even the commander responsible for the prison or for soldiers within the prison. The only two we suggest - the only two, we suggest, that come anywhere close to asserting otherwise are L-96 and L-64. What's L-96's claim? It comes to this: He claims Musliu told Murrizi to tie his hands. L-96 spoke in doubtful terms, we submit, of knowing what role Musliu actually played or what command he had. But may we make this submission: Based on the appeal of Josipovic, the appellant in the Kupreskic case, paragraphs 354 to 357 of that appeals judgement that even if, even if, this Chamber was attempted to accept L-96 on this, we submit that such simple instructions that could be given as much to an equal as well as a subordinate is not evidence of de jure or de facto command. I hope that's clear. L-64 accepted under cross-examination that he didn't know anything about the command structure. "I knew some names," he said, "but I didn't know what functions or grades they had." Page 4.708. And then we come to the beer incident claimed by L-64 and used by the Prosecution in their brief to support the proposition that Mr. Musliu had power to prevent or punish, sending a man home with a kidney problem because he was drinking beer, according to L-64. Well, even if true, and we suggest in fact L-64 is using this to divert from or cover up his own disarming, this incident cannot and should not be taken as proof that Musliu did indeed have power to prevent or punish the criminal conduct alleged against him in this indictment. L-64 also made claims that Musliu had authority to release prisoners. As I understand this case, we have had no evidence from any ex-prisoner or any KLA witness to support any releasing role for Musliu, nothing beyond L-64, nothing to confirm, still less to corroborate L-64 on these matters, who, as we shall be submitting in due course, one would not willingly convict one's dog on the evidence of L-64. So that deals with command. May I turn to individual responsibility. Evidence of personal participation in the camp's operation as against our client come from L-64 of course and L-96. Evidence of physical abuse meted out personally by Mr. Musliu comes, it is said from L-06, 12, 96, and the Bakracs. To say nothing of course of the allegations of murder of five individuals in the camp and one without of it, namely Ajet Gashi. Your Honours, rather than deal here with these matters, we think it would be more helpful to stick to the topics in the order in which they are raised in the final brief of the Prosecution, and therefore to return to personal participation in murder, as alleged, when we come to deal with crimes in the camp. We hope that is a more convenient and helpful way of setting out our submissions. The next heading in the Prosecution's brief is identification evidence. I've dealt with that and have nothing more to say about it. So I can move on to their next heading which is "KLA policy of targeting collaborators." I've touched on policy in the context of crimes against humanity already. This heading "KLA policy of targeting collaborators." We all remember this case was opened upon the basis that this was not a case against the KLA, but I move on. While accepting, as they must, that a warring party has the ability to deal with genuine, internal security threats, the Prosecution of course make the point that all such conduct must be subject to international humanitarian law in an armed conflict and no one could possibly disagree with that. The evidence of Safiulin, the Russian journalist, we suggest, demonstrates that up until the point of the alleged ill-treatment and worse of another member of his party, the conduct of that camera crew on that day in war, in a war zone, verged on the reckless, justifying at the very least in the heart of that war zone their being stopped, detained, and interrogated. Of course nothing I've just said should be taken as intending to or in fact excusing or explaining that which apparently then happened to their interpreter. Of course not. But likewise, we do suggest that routine stop and search of cars and so on at a roadblock for however long the roadblock was there cannot be any sense objectionable. The key question here of course is whilst their policy to target collaborators and did Musliu play his knowing part in implementing it? Your Honours, Mr. Krasniqi was on any view a significant figure in the KLA and an important witness in this trial. He was, as you will recall and you may agree, an intelligent man, an articulate man, a man who, may I say, clearly wished to present himself in a particular way to the Tribunal. It may have seemed at times, of course it's a matter entirely for you, that he was a touch arrogant, dismissive, and sometimes unfeeling and uncaring when dealing with some aspects of the collaborator issue. But clearly his definition of collaborators as recruits of the Serb security services, those, as he put it, who "served the violent Serb regime," justified to him detention, interrogation, and even, in extreme cases of course, their execution. He gave clear and unequivocal evidence, however, that it was no part of KLA to kidnap, torture, or murder the innocent, evidence we invite you to accept. We submit no such policy existed and the attempt to prove it via, for example, Krasniqi communique fails, in our submission. We respectfully remind the Trial Chamber to be wary of and skeptical about drawing positive and adverse inferences based on statements and declarations spewing confetti-like from both sides. The first casualty in war is the truth, and it may be helpful to keep that maxim in mind. Can I turn, then, to the Prosecutor's next heading and, you may think, the focal point of this trial: Crimes at the camp, the range of conduct of course alleged here against Mr. Musliu for which it is said he is responsible, both as a commander and as a perpetrator. What we'll do is we'll highlight and comment upon the Prosecution's position and then summarise and comment upon our own submissions, again, as it were, to enable you to lay them side by side. Kidnappings and arrest. Let's start with that because that's where they start. Part, of course, of the joint criminal enterprise. It's not suggested nor is there any evidence to suggest that Musliu was personally involved in this aspect. It's interesting, we observe, that considering, it is said, that others hold positions of authority and responsibility were involved in this aspect, it is curious, to say the least of it, that if so intimately concerned, there is not one piece of evidence that places Musliu at or near the scene of a single kidnapping or arrest. Conditions of detention. L-04 spoke of Qerqizi removing Ademi and Ahmeti, leaving two Serbs behind. May I interrupt myself. I asked that a glossary of the pseudonyms is placed before Your Honours. When we're dealing with this part of the evidence and this group of witnesses it's sometimes helpful just to remind ourselves who is who. L-04 did not know their names of the two men who removed Ademi and Ahmeti and was then asked, you may think, I certainly submit, one of the worst examples of a leading question in this whole trial. He's gone now, so I can be rude about him. Mr. Cayley said: "Q. Was it Qerqizi who took the two Serbs out?" Well, warned by Your Honour to take a little more care, the inevitable confirmatory answer was given by the witness. By the way, these men die, it is said, at the hands of Isak Musliu without there being any further evidence of any act carried out by him. But we'll come back to murder later. Interrogation is the next heading. Here it's alleged of course that Musliu was directly and personally implicated. And we'll look at what relevant witnesses had to say in due course in a little detail. But a comment, a comment here, if we may, on the Prosecution's recommended use of evidence by way of corroboration. This is an important example of the care that's required, we submit. As we've seen, Vojko Bakrac described, say the Prosecution, interrogation of Stamen Genov by Musliu, who referred to him as the sergeant. So the Prosecution advanced that there is corroboration for that piece of incriminating evidence. What do they point to? Genov's own recovered statement describing his work as a medic in the JNA. That's their submission, that that's corroboration of that identification of him as the man who beat Genov; it's not corroboration of anything, we submit, still less Musliu's involvement. Beatings and other abuse. The Genov beating is described as one that stands out. I've been through our critique of the Prosecution's position that it was carried out by someone "matching Musliu's description." And then they go on in the next breath to say that it was Musliu. That, we suggest, is an exercise in legalistic intellectual gamesmanship of the worst kind. This defendant is charged with murder, and the best they can do is suggest that he matches the description of a torturer. It's not good enough. Killings. By his own hand he's accused of killing the people familiar to us on the list, but not now Sinisa Blagojevic. With confidence, just taking Ademi and Ahmeti as examples, the Prosecution assert that they have proved beyond reasonable doubt that they were murdered after being taken out of the cowshed by Isak Musliu. They go further. In fact, they allege they were murdered by Isak Musliu. We'll come back to murder in a moment or two. So let's look at our submissions in response. And what we're looking at now of course is Musliu's liability pursuant to Article 7(1) in relation to murder and we're going to travel up the indictment for the last part of today. Counts 7 and 8, torture, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment, 3 to 6, imprisonment and cruel treatment, Counts 1 to 2. Your Honours, may I pause to say I won't finish this afternoon. If at any stage the Court feels it's heard too many speeches and too much today, I know the Court will stop me and I will find a moment. We appreciate it's difficult to listen to one voice, however attractive it may be, for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any thought at the moment, Mr. Topolski, as to how long you might be now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I won't finish tonight, but I'll finish within the first session tomorrow even if I stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The invitation is too tempting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I thought it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 2.15, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of September, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
